learningObjective: Draw the single conclusion that must be true given a short passage, distinguishing entailed inferences from statements that are merely consistent with or plausibly suggested by the text.
stem:
Passage: In the regional library network, any title held in the rare-books room is never available for home loan. Every title that can be reserved online can be borrowed for home loan. Some titles in the folklore collection can be reserved online, and every title in the folklore collection is either in the rare-books room or in the open-access hall, but no title is in both.

Which one of the following must be true on the basis of the passage alone?
choices: Every title in the folklore collection can be reserved online.
At least one title in the folklore collection is held in the open-access hall.
Every title in the rare-books room belongs to the folklore collection.
No title in the folklore collection can be borrowed for home loan.
No title in the open-access hall can be reserved online.
explanation: Chain the conditionals. Rare-books titles are never home-loanable; online-reservable titles are all home-loanable; therefore no rare-books title can be reserved online (contrapositive). Some folklore titles CAN be reserved online, so those particular folklore titles are not in the rare-books room. Since every folklore title is in either the rare-books room or the open-access hall (and not both), any folklore title that is not in the rare-books room must be in the open-access hall. Hence at least one folklore title is in the open-access hall — option B is guaranteed. The other options either overgeneralise from 'some' to 'all', assert unsupported exclusivity, or reverse a conditional.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect: the passage says only that SOME folklore titles can be reserved online; inferring 'every' is an illicit some-to-all generalisation.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: the online-reservable folklore titles cannot be in the rare-books room (they are home-loanable), so by the exclusive either/or they must be in the open-access hall — at least one such title exists.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect: this reverses the relationship — the passage never says rare-books titles are drawn from the folklore collection.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect: the folklore titles that can be reserved online are precisely the ones that CAN be borrowed for home loan, so 'no folklore title can be borrowed' is false.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect: nothing forbids open-access-hall titles from being reservable online; the passage constrains rare-books titles, not open-access ones.

subtopic: Identifying the main conclusion
learningObjective: Distinguish the main conclusion of an argument from its premises and from the opposing view it rebuts.
stem: Some city planners argue that building more roads reduces traffic congestion. Experience in several large cities suggests the opposite. When a new motorway opens, journey times fall at first, but within a few years they return to their previous level. This happens because the additional capacity attracts drivers who previously used other routes, travelled at other times, or did not drive at all. The lower effective cost of driving therefore generates extra trips until congestion once again rises to the point where it deters further use. Building more roads is thus not an effective long-term cure for congestion. Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the argument?
choices: Additional road capacity attracts drivers who previously used other routes or travelled at other times.
The lower effective cost of driving generates extra car trips.
Building more roads is not an effective long-term cure for traffic congestion.
Some city planners believe that building more roads reduces congestion.
When a new motorway opens, journey times initially fall before rising again.
explanation: The main conclusion is the claim that all other statements are offered to support. Here it is flagged by the connective 'thus' and is the endpoint of the described feedback mechanism (induced demand). The other statements are the opposing view being rebutted, an intermediate observation, or links in the causal chain that explain why the conclusion holds.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: This states the mechanism by which the new capacity fills up and functions as a premise; it explains the conclusion rather than being it. Misconception: mistaking an explanatory premise for the main claim.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: This is a further link in the causal chain (induced demand) that supports the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. Misconception: selecting a causal sub-claim instead of the overall point.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: Signalled by 'thus', this is the claim that every other statement in the passage is marshalled to support.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: This is the opposing position that the author sets out to rebut, not the author's own conclusion. Misconception: taking the view introduced by 'some argue' as the argument's conclusion.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: This is an intermediate empirical observation describing only the short-term effect; it is evidence offered in support, not the point the argument establishes. Misconception: treating a supporting fact as the conclusion.

subtopic: Flaw: necessary versus sufficient condition
learningObjective: Identify reasoning that treats a necessary condition as though it were sufficient.
stem: The regulations state that, to be awarded a distinction in the diploma, a student must score at least 70% in the final examination. Marco scored 82% in the final examination. The examiner therefore concluded that Marco will certainly be awarded a distinction. Which of the following best identifies the flaw in the examiner's reasoning?
choices: It assumes that any student who scores below 70% must be denied a distinction.
It treats a condition that is only required for a distinction as though it were enough to guarantee one.
It generalises from Marco's performance to that of the other students in the cohort.
It relies on the examiner's authority rather than on the published marking regulations.
It draws a conclusion about a single individual from a rule that is meant to apply to a whole group.
explanation: The regulation gives a necessary condition: scoring at least 70% is required for a distinction. The examiner treats it as a sufficient condition — enough to guarantee the distinction — overlooking that other requirements could also apply. Confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one is the flaw.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: If 70% is genuinely necessary, then scoring below it does entail no distinction — a valid contrapositive, not a flaw. Misconception: mistaking a valid inference for an unwarranted assumption.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: Scoring at least 70% is stated only as a requirement (a necessary condition); the examiner wrongly treats it as sufficient to guarantee the distinction, ignoring possible further requirements.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: The conclusion is about Marco alone; no claim is made about other students. Misconception: mislabelling the error as a hasty generalisation.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: The examiner appeals to the marking regulation, not to personal authority. Misconception: mislabelling the error as an appeal to authority.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: A general rule can legitimately be applied to an individual, so this is not the error. Misconception: assuming that rules cannot be used to reason about single cases.

subtopic: Strengthening an argument (controlling confounders)
learningObjective: Recognise how matched groups and blinding strengthen a causal conclusion by removing confounders and bias.
stem: A pharmaceutical company claims that its new painkiller, Analgex, is more effective than the standard drug. In a clinical trial, patients who took Analgex reported greater pain relief on average than those who took the standard drug, and the company concluded that Analgex is the more effective painkiller. Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the company's conclusion?
choices: Analgex is considerably more expensive to manufacture than the standard drug.
A separate trial run by a different company found the standard drug to be highly effective.
Before the trial, patients in the Analgex group were told that they were receiving a promising new treatment.
The patients who took Analgex were, on average, several years younger than those who took the standard drug.
The two groups were closely matched for injury type and initial pain severity, and neither the patients nor the assessors knew which drug each patient received.
explanation: The conclusion is justified only if the greater average relief is due to the drug itself rather than to differences between the groups or to expectation effects. Matching the groups on relevant baseline factors and keeping both patients and assessors blind removes the main confounders and placebo/observer biases, so the observed difference is more credibly attributable to Analgex.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: Manufacturing cost is irrelevant to which drug relieves pain more effectively. Misconception: importing an irrelevant consideration into a claim about effectiveness.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: A separate finding that the standard drug works well says nothing about the head-to-head comparison in this trial. Misconception: treating an isolated fact about one drug as evidence for a comparative claim.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Telling patients they are receiving a promising treatment invites a placebo/expectation effect, providing an alternative cause and weakening the conclusion. Misconception: mistaking a bias-introducing factor for support.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: An age difference introduces a confounder that offers a rival explanation for the result, weakening rather than strengthening the conclusion. Misconception: assuming any extra detail about the treatment group supports the claim.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: Matched baseline characteristics plus double-blinding rule out confounding and placebo/observer effects, so the difference in reported relief is more plausibly caused by the drug.

subtopic: Matching / assignment deduction
learningObjective: Solve a constraint-based assignment puzzle by chaining deductions to a unique solution.
stem: Four colleagues — Ada, Ben, Cara and Dan — each ordered a different drink from the choices coffee, tea, juice and water. The following facts are known: Ada ordered neither coffee nor tea; Ben ordered neither juice nor water; Cara ordered tea; Dan did not order juice. Who ordered the water?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: Cara ordered tea. Ben ordered neither juice nor water, and tea is already taken, so Ben ordered coffee. That leaves juice and water for Ada and Dan. Dan did not order juice, so Dan ordered water and Ada ordered juice.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: The four constraints determine a unique solution, so the answer is fixed. Misconception: assuming the puzzle is under-determined without completing the chain of deductions.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: Ben is forced onto coffee, because he can take neither juice nor water and tea belongs to Cara. Misconception: overlooking that tea is already assigned when placing Ben.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Cara is explicitly assigned tea. Misconception: misreading a fixed assignment given directly in the clues.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: Ben must take coffee, leaving juice and water for Ada and Dan; because Dan cannot take juice, Dan takes water.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Ada cannot take coffee or tea; once Ben takes coffee and Cara tea, Ada is left with juice or water, and since Dan cannot take juice, Ada must take juice, not water. Misconception: stopping before applying the constraint on Dan.

subtopic: Simpson's paradox / weighted-average reversal
learningObjective: Explain a rate reversal between aggregated and disaggregated data using differential case-mix (Simpson's paradox).
stem: A hospital reviews two surgeons. Overall, Surgeon X has a higher patient survival rate than Surgeon Y. However, when patients are split into 'high-risk' and 'low-risk' groups, Surgeon Y has a higher survival rate than Surgeon X within the high-risk group and also within the low-risk group. Which of the following, if true, best explains this apparent contradiction?
choices: Surgeon X treated a larger total number of patients than Surgeon Y.
Survival rates are generally higher for low-risk patients than for high-risk patients.
Within each risk group, Surgeon Y's survival rate exceeded Surgeon X's by only a small margin.
When the two surgeons' patients are combined, the high-risk group is larger than the low-risk group.
Surgeon Y operated on a much higher proportion of high-risk patients than Surgeon X did.
explanation: Surgeon Y can be better in every subgroup yet worse overall if Y's overall rate is a weighted average dominated by the low-survival high-risk patients. This occurs when Y treats a much larger share of high-risk patients than X does: the difference in case-mix, not surgical skill, drags Y's overall rate below X's. This is the mechanism of Simpson's paradox.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: The total number of patients does not by itself determine the direction of the averaged rates. Misconception: believing a larger sample alone can reverse a comparison.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: This is part of the setup (a background fact); on its own it does not explain why Y leads in both subgroups yet trails overall — that also requires a difference in case-mix between the surgeons. Misconception: mistaking a background premise for the explanation.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: The size of each within-group margin does not create the reversal; the reversal is produced by unequal weighting of the subgroups. Misconception: attributing the paradox to small subgroup differences rather than to case-mix.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: The combined-group composition is irrelevant; what matters is the difference in case-mix between the two surgeons, not the overall totals. Misconception: confusing the overall group size with the differential allocation between surgeons.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: If Y treats far more high-risk (low-survival) patients, Y's overall rate is a weighted average pulled down by that group, so Y can trail X overall while leading within each subgroup — the mechanism of Simpson's paradox.

subtopic: Absolute-value equations
learningObjective: Solve an absolute-value equation by splitting into cases and count the distinct real solutions.
stem: How many distinct real values of x satisfy the equation |x² − 4| = 3 ?
explanation: The equation splits into two cases. Case 1: x² − 4 = 3 ⇒ x² = 7 ⇒ x = ±√7 (two real solutions). Case 2: x² − 4 = −3 ⇒ x² = 1 ⇒ x = ±1 (two more real solutions). Because √7 ≈ 2.65 and 1 are all distinct, there are four distinct real solutions in total.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct. ±√7 and ±1 give four distinct real roots.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 3 would require one repeated root, but none of the four values coincide.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. Solutions clearly exist, so 0 is wrong.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 2 results from solving only the case x² − 4 = 3 (or only x² = 1).
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. 1 ignores that each x² value yields two opposite roots.

subtopic: Combinatorial probability with 'at least'
learningObjective: Compute an 'at least' probability using combinations and the complement rule.
stem: A committee of 4 people is chosen at random from a group of 5 men and 4 women. What is the probability that the committee contains at least 2 women?
explanation: The total number of committees is C(9,4) = 126. Use the complement of 'fewer than 2 women': committees with 0 women = C(5,4) = 5; committees with exactly 1 woman = C(4,1)·C(5,3) = 4·10 = 40. So committees with at least 2 women = 126 − 5 − 40 = 81. The probability is 81/126 = 9/14.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. 3/7 = 54/126 does not match any correct combination of the cases.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 20/63 = 40/126 is the probability of exactly one woman only.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 5/14 = 45/126 is the probability of the complement (0 or 1 woman) after simplification error.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. 2/3 = 84/126 slightly over-counts and is not obtained from the correct case analysis.

subtopic: Change-of-base substitution in a logarithmic equation
learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by reducing it to a quadratic through a substitution and combine the roots.
stem: Consider the equation log₂(x) + logₓ(2) = 5/2, defined for x > 0 with x ≠ 1. What is the product of all real solutions of this equation?
explanation: Let t = log₂(x). By change of base logₓ(2) = 1/log₂(x) = 1/t, so the equation becomes t + 1/t = 5/2, i.e. 2t² − 5t + 2 = 0, giving t = 2 or t = 1/2. Hence x = 2² = 4 or x = 2^(1/2) = √2, both valid (positive, ≠ 1). Their product is 4·√2 = 4√2. Equivalently, the product equals 2^(t₁+t₂) = 2^(5/2) = 4√2.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: x = 4 and x = √2 give a product of 4√2 = 2^(5/2).
optionAnalysis.B: Keeps only t = 2 and squares it, or multiplies the exponents (2 · 1/2 mishandled) to reach 2³ = 8.
optionAnalysis.C: Keeps only the root t = 1/2, reporting the single solution √2.
optionAnalysis.D: Uses the product of the t-values (2 · 1/2 = 1) as an exponent: 2¹ = 2, misapplying the exponent law.
optionAnalysis.E: Adds the two solutions (4 + √2) instead of multiplying them.

subtopic: Hypergeometric probability without replacement
learningObjective: Compute a probability for sampling without replacement using combinations rather than independent trials.
stem: A box contains 12 electronic components, of which exactly 4 are defective. Three components are drawn at random simultaneously (that is, without replacement). What is the probability that exactly one of the three drawn components is defective?
explanation: Because the draws are simultaneous, use combinations. Favourable outcomes = choosing 1 of the 4 defective and 2 of the 8 good: C(4,1)·C(8,2) = 4·28 = 112. Total outcomes = C(12,3) = 220. Probability = 112/220 = 28/55. Independent-trial (with-replacement) reasoning is invalid here because the composition changes with each draw.

optionAnalysis.A: Uses C(4,1)/C(12,3) = 4/220 = 1/55-type slip, omitting the C(8,2) factor (here rounded to 4/55).
optionAnalysis.B: Halves the favourable count (uses C(8,2)/2 or forgets the factor 2 in a pair count), giving 56/220 = 14/55.
optionAnalysis.D: Treats draws as independent with p = 1/3 defective: 3·(1/3)(2/3)² = 27/64-style with-replacement error.
optionAnalysis.E: Simply reports the defective fraction 4/12 = 1/3, ignoring the 'exactly one of three' condition.

subtopic: Counting real solutions of an absolute-value quadratic equation
learningObjective: Solve an equation containing an absolute value of a quadratic by case analysis and discard extraneous roots.
stem: How many distinct real solutions does the equation |x² − 4| = x + 2 have?
explanation: First, the right side must be non-negative, so x ≥ −2. Case 1 (|x| ≥ 2, where x² − 4 ≥ 0): x² − 4 = x + 2 ⇒ x² − x − 6 = 0 ⇒ x = 3 or x = −2; both satisfy x ≥ −2 and x² − 4 ≥ 0, so both are valid. Case 2 (|x| < 2, where x² − 4 < 0): −(x² − 4) = x + 2 ⇒ x² + x − 2 = 0 ⇒ x = 1 or x = −2; only x = 1 lies in |x| < 2 (x = −2 is a boundary already counted). The distinct valid solutions are x = −2, 1, 3 — three in total.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: valid roots are x = −2, 1, 3, giving three distinct solutions.
optionAnalysis.B: Counts all four algebraic roots (3, −2, 1, −2) without noticing x = −2 repeats and without the x ≥ −2 check.
optionAnalysis.C: Discards x = −2 for wrongly requiring x > −2 (strict), keeping only x = 3 or only x = 1.
optionAnalysis.D: Concludes no solution by assuming |x² − 4| can never equal a linear expression, skipping case analysis.
optionAnalysis.E: Solves only the case x² − 4 = x + 2 (roots 3 and −2), missing the sign-flipped case that yields x = 1.

subtopic: Law of cosines with the circumradius (law of sines)
learningObjective: Integrate the law of cosines and the law of sines to find the circumscribed-circle radius of a triangle.
stem: In triangle ABC the angle at vertex A measures 60°, the side AB = 8 and the side AC = 5. What is the radius of the circle circumscribed about the triangle?
explanation: The side opposite A is BC = a. By the law of cosines, a² = AB² + AC² − 2·AB·AC·cos 60° = 64 + 25 − 2·8·5·(1/2) = 89 − 40 = 49, so a = 7. By the law of sines, 2R = a/sin A = 7/sin 60° = 7/(√3/2) = 14/√3, hence R = 7/√3 = 7√3/3.

optionAnalysis.A: Uses R = a·(√3/2)/... i.e. multiplies by sin A instead of dividing, giving 7√3/2.
optionAnalysis.B: Uses 2R = a/sin A but reports 2R = 14/√3 = 14√3/3 as R, forgetting to halve.
optionAnalysis.C: Divides by an extra factor of 2, using R = a/(4 sin A) and getting 7√3/6.
optionAnalysis.D: Sets R = a/2 = 7/2, forgetting the sin A denominator (treating a as a diameter).
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: a = 7 and R = a/(2 sin A) = 7/√3 = 7√3/3.

subtopic: Exponential equation reducible to a quadratic
learningObjective: Solve an exponential equation by substitution and sum its real solutions.
stem: What is the sum of all real solutions x of the equation 2^(2x) − 5·2^x + 4 = 0 ?
explanation: Let u = 2^x (so u > 0). The equation becomes u² − 5u + 4 = 0, which factors as (u − 1)(u − 4) = 0, giving u = 1 or u = 4. Then 2^x = 1 ⇒ x = 0, and 2^x = 4 ⇒ x = 2. Both are valid (u > 0). The sum of the solutions is 0 + 2 = 2.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 5 is the sum of the roots in u (1 + 4), not the sum of the x-values.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 3 does not correspond to the solution set.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 6 mis-solves 2^x = 4 as x = 4 or similar.
optionAnalysis.D: CORRECT: the solutions are x = 0 and x = 2, summing to 2.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0 is only one of the two solutions (x = 0), not their sum.

subtopic: Probability of an even product (complement)
learningObjective: Compute the probability of an even product using the complement (all-odd) and combinations.
stem: Two distinct integers are chosen at random from the set {1, 2, 3, …, 10}. What is the probability that their product is even?
explanation: The product is even unless BOTH chosen numbers are odd. There are 5 odd numbers {1,3,5,7,9}, so the number of all-odd pairs is C(5,2) = 10, out of C(10,2) = 45 total pairs. P(product odd) = 10/45 = 2/9, so P(product even) = 1 − 2/9 = 7/9.

optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 5/9 does not follow from the correct count of pairs.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 2/9 is the probability the product is ODD (both numbers odd), i.e. the complement.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 4/9 mis-counts the favourable or total pairs.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 1/2 assumes even/odd are equally likely, ignoring that only an all-odd pair gives an odd product.

subtopic: Sum of an infinite geometric series (repeated-dose steady state)
learningObjective: Model a repeated-dose accumulation process as an infinite geometric series and evaluate its steady-state sum.
stem: A patient is treated with a drug taken as a single 60 mg dose at the same time every day. Over each 24-hour interval the body eliminates 75% of the drug present, so that just before the next dose only 25% of the previous amount remains in the body. Assuming this pattern continues indefinitely, what amount of drug is present in the body immediately after a dose is taken in the long-term (steady) state?
explanation: Let L be the amount present immediately after a dose in the steady state. Each day the previous amount decays to 25% of itself, then a fresh 60 mg is added, so at equilibrium L = 60 + 0.25 L. Hence 0.75 L = 60 and L = 80 mg. Equivalently, the doses form an infinite geometric series 60 + 60(0.25) + 60(0.25)^2 + ... with first term 60 and ratio r = 0.25, summing to 60/(1 − 0.25) = 80 mg.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: takes the steady-state level to equal a single dose (60 mg), ignoring the drug carried over from previous doses — i.e. omitting the accumulation entirely.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: reports the trough level just before the next dose (0.25 × 80 = 20 mg), misreading 'immediately after' as 'immediately before'.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: at equilibrium L = 60 + 0.25L gives L = 60/(1 − 0.25) = 80 mg, the sum of the infinite geometric series with a = 60, r = 0.25.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses the eliminated fraction r = 0.75 instead of the retained fraction 0.25 in the sum, giving 60/(1 − 0.75) = 240 mg.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: adds only the first two doses (60 + 0.25×60 = 75 mg), truncating the geometric series after two terms instead of summing it to its limit.

subtopic: Vieta's formulas: sum of squares of the roots of a cubic
learningObjective: Apply Vieta's formulas to evaluate a symmetric function (the sum of the squares) of the roots of a cubic without solving it.
stem: Let p, q and r be the three roots (real or complex) of the cubic equation 2x^3 − 3x^2 + 4x − 5 = 0. What is the value of p^2 + q^2 + r^2?
explanation: For 2x^3 − 3x^2 + 4x − 5 = 0, Vieta's formulas give p + q + r = 3/2, pq + pr + qr = 4/2 = 2, and pqr = 5/2. Using the identity p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = (p + q + r)^2 − 2(pq + pr + qr) = (3/2)^2 − 2(2) = 9/4 − 4 = −7/4. (The value is negative because two of the roots are complex conjugates; the symmetric function is nonetheless real.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: computes only (p + q + r)^2 = (3/2)^2 = 9/4, forgetting to subtract the 2(pq + pr + qr) term.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: divides only the sum of roots by the leading coefficient but forgets to divide the pairwise sum, giving (3/2)^2 − 2(4) = −23/4.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = (3/2)^2 − 2(2) = 9/4 − 4 = −7/4, applying Vieta's formulas with the leading coefficient 2.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: reads the coefficients directly as the symmetric sums (sum = 3, pairwise sum = 4), ignoring the leading coefficient 2, giving 3^2 − 2×4 = 1.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: uses the wrong sign, (p + q + r)^2 + 2(pq + pr + qr) = 9/4 + 4 = 25/4, adding rather than subtracting the pairwise term.

subtopic: Rational inequality solved by sign analysis
learningObjective: Solve a rational inequality by collecting terms on one side and analysing the sign of the resulting quotient, respecting domain restrictions.
stem: Determine the complete solution set of the inequality (2x − 1)/(x + 3) ≥ 1.
explanation: Move everything to one side: (2x − 1)/(x + 3) − 1 ≥ 0, i.e. (2x − 1 − (x + 3))/(x + 3) ≥ 0, which simplifies to (x − 4)/(x + 3) ≥ 0. The critical values are x = 4 (numerator zero, included) and x = −3 (denominator zero, excluded). A sign chart shows the quotient is positive for x < −3 and for x > 4, and equals 0 at x = 4. Hence the solution set is (−∞, −3) ∪ [4, +∞).

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: multiplies both sides by (x + 3) as if it were always positive, obtaining 2x − 1 ≥ x + 3 → x ≥ 4, and loses the branch where the denominator is negative.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: includes x = −3, but there the denominator is zero and the expression is undefined, so −3 must be excluded.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: rearranging gives (x − 4)/(x + 3) ≥ 0; the quotient is non-negative for x < −3 or x ≥ 4, so the solution is (−∞, −3) ∪ [4, +∞).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: excludes x = 4, but the inequality is non-strict (≥) and the numerator (x − 4) is zero there, so x = 4 must be included.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: selects the interval between the critical values, where the quotient is actually negative — the sign of the quotient has been reversed.

subtopic: System of exponential equations via common-base exponents
learningObjective: Solve a system of exponential equations by rewriting each term to a common base and equating exponents to form and solve a linear system.
stem: Real numbers x and y satisfy the system: 2^x · 8^y = 2^11 and 9^x / 3^y = 3. What is the value of x + y?
explanation: Rewrite with common bases. First equation: 2^x · 2^(3y) = 2^(x + 3y) = 2^11, so x + 3y = 11. Second equation: 3^(2x) / 3^y = 3^(2x − y) = 3^1, so 2x − y = 1. From the second, y = 2x − 1; substituting: x + 3(2x − 1) = 11 → 7x − 3 = 11 → x = 2, and then y = 3. Therefore x + y = 5.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: treats 8^y as 2^y (dropping the exponent 3 in 8 = 2^3), so the first equation reads x + y = 11 directly.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: rewriting to bases 2 and 3 gives x + 3y = 11 and 2x − y = 1, whose solution is x = 2, y = 3, so x + y = 5.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: solves the system correctly to x = 2, y = 3 but reports x alone instead of the requested sum x + y.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: simply adds the two right-hand exponents (11 from 2^11 and 1 from 3^1) to get 12, without solving the system.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: treats 9^x as 3^x (dropping the exponent 2 in 9 = 3^2), giving the second equation as x − y = 1 and hence x + y = 6.

subtopic: Interplay of arithmetic and geometric progressions
learningObjective: Combine the defining conditions of arithmetic and geometric progressions to determine an unknown common ratio.
stem: In an arithmetic progression with non-zero common difference, the first term is 3, and the first, second and fifth terms are (in that order) three consecutive terms of a geometric progression. What is the common ratio of that geometric progression?
explanation: Let the arithmetic progression have first term a = 3 and common difference d. The first, second and fifth terms are a, a + d and a + 4d. For these to be consecutive terms of a geometric progression, (a + d)^2 = a(a + 4d). Expanding: a^2 + 2ad + d^2 = a^2 + 4ad, so d^2 − 2ad = 0, i.e. d(d − 2a) = 0. Since d ≠ 0, d = 2a = 6. The three geometric terms are 3, 9, 27, so the common ratio is 27/9 = 9/3 = 3.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: computes d/a = 6/3 = 2, confusing the relationship between the common difference and the first term with the geometric common ratio.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: the geometric condition gives d = 6, producing terms 3, 9, 27 with common ratio 9/3 = 3.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: inverts the ratio, dividing an earlier term by a later one (3/9) instead of a later term by an earlier one.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: reports the second geometric term (a + d = 9) itself rather than the ratio between successive terms.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: reports the common difference d = 6 of the arithmetic progression instead of the common ratio of the geometric progression.

subtopic: Infinite geometric series: sum and sum of squares
learningObjective: Set up and solve simultaneous equations from the sum and the sum of squares of an infinite geometric series.
stem: An infinite geometric series has first term a and common ratio r with |r| < 1. The sum of the series is 9, and the sum of the squares of its terms is 40.5. What is the value of the common ratio r?
explanation: The sum of the series is a/(1 − r) = 9. The squares of the terms form a geometric series with first term a² and ratio r², so their sum is a²/(1 − r²) = 40.5. Substituting a = 9(1 − r) into the second equation: [9(1 − r)]²/(1 − r²) = 81(1 − r)²/[(1 − r)(1 + r)] = 81(1 − r)/(1 + r) = 40.5. Hence (1 − r)/(1 + r) = 0.5, giving 1 − r = 0.5 + 0.5r, so 1.5r = 0.5 and r = 1/3. (Check: a = 6, sum = 6/(2/3) = 9; sum of squares = 36/(8/9) = 40.5.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/9 confuses r with r² or misreads the ratio of the two sums.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: r = 1/4 comes from mishandling the 1 − r² factorisation (e.g. treating it as (1 − r)²).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: r = 2/3 makes the terms fall off too slowly; the sum of squares would exceed 40.5.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: r = 1/2 gives (1 − r)/(1 + r) = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3, not 0.5, so the sum of squares would not be 40.5.

subtopic: Change of momentum on rebound
learningObjective: Apply the impulse–momentum theorem to a rebounding object, handling the change of direction correctly.
stem: A 0.20 kg ball travelling horizontally at 10 m/s strikes a rigid vertical wall head-on and rebounds horizontally at 8.0 m/s in the opposite direction. The ball is in contact with the wall for 0.020 s. What is the magnitude of the average force exerted by the wall on the ball?
explanation: Take the initial direction as positive. The ball's momentum changes from +(0.20)(10) = +2.0 kg·m/s to −(0.20)(8.0) = −1.6 kg·m/s because it reverses direction. The change in momentum is Δp = −1.6 − (+2.0) = −3.6 kg·m/s, magnitude 3.6 kg·m/s. The average force is |Δp|/Δt = 3.6 / 0.020 = 180 N.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. 20 N comes from using the difference in speeds (10 − 8 = 2 m/s) and ignoring the direction reversal.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 100 N corresponds to bringing the ball only to rest from 10 m/s (Δp = 2.0), not to rebounding.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. 360 N doubles the correct impulse, e.g. by adding the speeds and also mishandling the mass or time.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 90 N uses only the rebound speed (8 m/s) and ignores the incoming momentum.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct. Accounts for the reversal: |Δp| = 3.6 kg·m/s, so F = 3.6/0.020 = 180 N.

subtopic: Reversible adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas
learningObjective: Use the adiabatic relation T·V^(γ−1) = constant to find the final temperature of a monatomic ideal gas.
stem: A fixed quantity of an ideal monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) expands reversibly and adiabatically until its volume has doubled. If the initial absolute temperature of the gas is T, what is its final absolute temperature?
explanation: For a reversible adiabatic process, T·V^(γ−1) is constant, so T1·V1^(γ−1) = T2·V2^(γ−1). With γ = 5/3, the exponent γ − 1 = 2/3. Hence T2 = T1·(V1/V2)^(2/3) = T·(1/2)^(2/3) = T / 2^(2/3) = T / ∛4 (since 2^(2/3) = (2²)^(1/3) = ∛4 ≈ 1.59). The gas cools to about 0.63 T.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. T/2 would follow from an isothermal-style or incorrect linear assumption, ignoring γ.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 2T/3 has no basis in the adiabatic relation.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. T/4 uses an exponent of 2 instead of 2/3.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. T·∛2 makes the gas warm on expansion, which is impossible for an adiabatic expansion doing work.

subtopic: banked curve with friction, maximum speed
learningObjective: Combine banking angle and friction to find the maximum safe speed on a curved road, integrating Newton's second law in two directions.
stem: A curved road of radius 50 m is banked at an angle such that tan(theta) = 0.75. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is 0.25. Take g = 10 m/s^2. What is the maximum speed at which a car can round the curve without sliding outward?
explanation: For the maximum speed, friction acts down the slope (preventing outward slide). Resolving along horizontal and vertical: v_max^2 = rg(tan theta + mu)/(1 - mu tan theta) = 50*10*(0.75 + 0.25)/(1 - 0.25*0.75) = 500*(1.00)/(1 - 0.1875) = 500/0.8125 = 615.4, so v_max = 24.8 m/s ≈ 25 m/s. The key traps are the sign of mu (down-slope at maximum speed) and the denominator term (1 - mu tan theta).

optionAnalysis.A: 22 m/s ignores the denominator correction, using v^2 = rg(tan theta + mu) = 500 → 22.4 m/s.
optionAnalysis.B: 15 m/s comes from subtracting mu from tan theta (friction up-slope, the minimum-speed case) instead of adding.
optionAnalysis.C: 19 m/s uses the frictionless banking speed v^2 = rg tan theta = 375 → 19.4 m/s, ignoring friction.
optionAnalysis.D: 30 m/s reverses the friction sign, using (tan theta + mu)/(1 + ... ) errors or adding rather than the correct combination, overestimating.
optionAnalysis.E: CORRECT: v_max^2 = rg(tan theta + mu)/(1 - mu tan theta) = 500(1.00)/(0.8125) ≈ 615, v ≈ 25 m/s.

subtopic: two-dimensional collision and kinetic-energy loss
learningObjective: Apply conservation of momentum to a perpendicular collision and compute the fraction of kinetic energy lost.
stem: On a frictionless horizontal surface, a 3.0 kg puck moving east at 4.0 m/s strikes a 1.0 kg puck moving north at 6.0 m/s. The two pucks stick together after impact. What fraction of the total initial kinetic energy is lost in the collision?
explanation: Momentum is conserved in the collision. Before impact: p_x = (3.0)(4.0) = 12 kg·m/s (east), p_y = (1.0)(6.0) = 6.0 kg·m/s (north). The 4.0 kg combined mass moves with momentum p = √(12² + 6²) = √180 ≈ 13.4 kg·m/s, so v = 13.4/4.0 ≈ 3.35 m/s. Initial KE = ½(3.0)(4.0²) + ½(1.0)(6.0²) = 24 + 18 = 42 J. Final KE = ½(4.0)(3.35²) ≈ 22.5 J. Fraction of KE lost = (42 − 22.5)/42 ≈ 0.46, i.e. about 0.45.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 0.33 does not follow from a correct momentum-and-energy calculation.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 0.55 is close to the fraction of KE RETAINED (22.5/42 ≈ 0.54), i.e. the complement of the answer — a classic retained-vs-lost slip.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.25 typically comes from adding the momentum components as scalars (12 + 6 = 18) instead of using the Pythagorean resultant.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.70 overestimates the loss, e.g. by assuming one puck is brought to rest.

subtopic: buoyancy combined with gas law under submersion
learningObjective: Integrate hydrostatic pressure, the ideal gas law and Archimedes' principle to determine the buoyant force on a compressible bubble at depth.
stem: A small air bubble is released at the bottom of a fresh-water lake where the absolute pressure is 3.0 atm and rises to a depth where the absolute pressure is 1.5 atm. Temperature is constant. If the buoyant force on the bubble at the deeper point is F, what is the buoyant force at the shallower point? (The bubble remains fully submerged and behaves as an ideal gas.)
explanation: Buoyant force equals the weight of water displaced, F_b = rho_water * g * V_bubble, so F_b is proportional to the bubble volume V. At constant temperature Boyle's law gives P*V = constant, so V is inversely proportional to absolute pressure. Going from 3.0 atm to 1.5 atm halves the pressure, doubling the volume, hence doubling the buoyant force. F_shallow = 2F. The water density is essentially constant, so the entire change comes from the gas expansion.

optionAnalysis.A: CORRECT: V ∝ 1/P (Boyle), pressure halves so V doubles, and F_b ∝ V, giving 2F.
optionAnalysis.B: 4F squares the pressure ratio, treating volume as inversely proportional to P^2.
optionAnalysis.C: F/2 applies the pressure ratio directly to force (F ∝ P), the inverse of the correct relation.
optionAnalysis.D: 3F/2 uses the pressure ratio 3.0/2.0 incorrectly or averages pressures instead of applying Boyle's law.
optionAnalysis.E: F assumes the bubble volume is unchanged, ignoring gas expansion as pressure drops.

subtopic: capacitor charging energy and steady-state current in RC network
learningObjective: Analyse a mixed resistor-capacitor circuit at steady state, finding the voltage across a capacitor and the energy it stores.
stem: A 12 V ideal battery is connected in series with a 2.0 ohm resistor R1, which then connects to a parallel combination of a 4.0 ohm resistor R2 and a branch containing a 6.0 ohm resistor R3 in series with a 5.0 microfarad capacitor C. After a long time (steady state), what energy is stored in the capacitor?
explanation: At steady state no current flows through the capacitor branch, so no current flows through R3 and there is no voltage drop across R3. The capacitor therefore charges to the full voltage across R2. With the R3-C branch carrying no current, the circuit reduces to R1 (2.0 ohm) in series with R2 (4.0 ohm) across 12 V. Current I = 12/(2.0+4.0) = 2.0 A. Voltage across R2 = I*R2 = 2.0*4.0 = 8.0 V. Since no current flows in R3, the capacitor voltage equals the voltage across R2 = 8.0 V. Energy = (1/2)C V^2 = 0.5 * 5.0e-6 * 8.0^2 = 0.5*5.0e-6*64 = 160e-6 J = 160 microjoules.

optionAnalysis.A: 40 uJ uses V_C = 4.0 V, treating the R2 value directly as a voltage.
optionAnalysis.B: 90 uJ places a fictitious voltage drop across R3 (using 6 V), forgetting that no current flows there at steady state.
optionAnalysis.C: 250 uJ uses V_C = 10 V, obtained by dropping only R1 (12 - 2 = 10) instead of solving the divider.
optionAnalysis.D: CORRECT: steady-state V_C = 8.0 V across R2; U = (1/2)(5.0 uF)(8.0)^2 = 160 uJ.
optionAnalysis.E: 360 uJ uses the full 12 V across the capacitor, ignoring the drop across R1.

subtopic: motional EMF and induced power with wave-speed check
learningObjective: Compute motional EMF, induced current and dissipated power for a conducting rod on rails in a magnetic field, and identify the force needed to maintain constant speed.
stem: A conducting rod of length 0.50 m slides at a constant speed of 4.0 m/s along frictionless horizontal rails connected by a 2.0 ohm resistor. A uniform magnetic field of 0.80 T is directed vertically, perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The rod and rails have negligible resistance. What external force must be applied to the rod to keep its speed constant?
explanation: The motional EMF is ε = BLv = (0.80)(0.50)(4.0) = 1.6 V. The induced current is I = ε/R = 1.6/2.0 = 0.80 A. The magnetic force on the current-carrying rod is F = BIL = (0.80)(0.80)(0.50) = 0.32 N, directed opposite to the motion. To keep the rod moving at constant speed, the applied force must exactly balance this retarding force: 0.32 N. (Equivalently F = B²L²v/R = 0.32 N.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 0.64 N is exactly double the correct value — a common error from double-counting a factor (e.g. F = 2BIL).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 0.16 N is half the correct value, e.g. from omitting a factor.
optionAnalysis.C: CORRECT: F = BIL = B²L²v/R = 0.32 N balances the induced retarding force.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 2.56 N is a gross overestimate (factor of 8).
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 1.28 N is four times too large.

subtopic: Energy dissipated when capacitors are connected (charge sharing)
learningObjective: Use charge conservation to find the final voltage of two connected capacitors and the energy dissipated in the process.
stem: A 2.0 μF capacitor is charged to 100 V and then disconnected from the battery. Its two terminals are then connected, in parallel, to an initially uncharged 3.0 μF capacitor. Once the system reaches equilibrium, how much energy has been dissipated?
explanation: Charge is conserved (no battery): Q = C₁V₁ = (2.0 μF)(100 V) = 200 μC. After connection the capacitors share this charge across a total capacitance of 2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0 μF, giving a common voltage V′ = 200 μC / 5.0 μF = 40 V. Initial energy = ½C₁V₁² = ½(2.0 μF)(100²) = 10 mJ. Final energy = ½(5.0 μF)(40²) = 4 mJ. Energy dissipated = 10 − 4 = 6 mJ. Energy is always lost this way (as heat/radiation), regardless of connecting-wire resistance.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 10 mJ is the INITIAL stored energy, not the amount dissipated.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: energy is not conserved here — connecting charged to uncharged capacitors always dissipates energy.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 4 mJ is the FINAL stored energy, not the energy dissipated.
optionAnalysis.D: CORRECT: 10 mJ initial − 4 mJ final = 6 mJ dissipated.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 2 mJ underestimates the loss (e.g. from a wrong final voltage).

subtopic: Motion on a rough incline (energy/kinematics)
learningObjective: Combine the gravitational and frictional force components on an incline to find the speed after a given displacement.
stem: A 1.0 kg block is released from rest and slides down a rough incline that makes an angle of 37° with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between block and incline is 0.25. What is the block's speed after it has slid 2.0 m along the incline? (Take g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.60, cos 37° = 0.80.)
explanation: The acceleration down the incline is a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) = 10(0.60 − 0.25 × 0.80) = 10(0.60 − 0.20) = 4.0 m/s². Starting from rest over a distance s = 2.0 m, v² = 2as = 2(4.0)(2.0) = 16, so v = 4.0 m/s.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 2.8 m/s corresponds to an acceleration of ~2 m/s², e.g. from doubling the friction term.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 3.2 m/s uses too small a net acceleration.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 5.7 m/s uses no friction AND double the distance, or otherwise inflates the acceleration.
optionAnalysis.D: CORRECT: a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) = 4.0 m/s², so v = √(2·4·2) = 4.0 m/s.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 4.9 m/s is the frictionless result (a = g sin θ = 6.0 m/s², v = √24), ignoring friction.

subtopic: Impulse–momentum theorem from a force–time graph
learningObjective: Compute the impulse of a time-varying force as the area under a force–time graph and apply the impulse–momentum theorem to find the resulting speed.
stem: A trolley of mass 2.0 kg rests on a straight, frictionless horizontal track. A single horizontal force is then applied to it. The force is zero at t = 0, rises linearly to 6.0 N at t = 2.0 s, remains constant at 6.0 N until t = 5.0 s, and then drops immediately to zero. What is the speed of the trolley just after t = 5.0 s?
explanation: The impulse equals the area under the force–time graph: a triangle for the ramp, ½ × 2.0 s × 6.0 N = 6.0 N·s, plus a rectangle for the constant phase, 6.0 N × 3.0 s = 18 N·s, giving a total impulse of 24 N·s. By the impulse–momentum theorem this equals the change of momentum. Starting from rest, p = 24 kg·m/s, so v = p/m = 24 / 2.0 = 12 m/s.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: counts only the constant-force rectangle (impulse 18 N·s) and omits the initial ramp, giving 18/2.0 = 9.0 m/s.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: treats the area under a force–time graph as work in joules and sets ½mv² = 24 J, confusing impulse with energy (v = √24 ≈ 4.9 m/s).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: treats the force as constant at its peak value 6.0 N for the whole 5.0 s (impulse 30 N·s), giving 15 m/s.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: counts only the triangular ramp (impulse 6.0 N·s) and ignores the constant-force phase, giving 6.0/2.0 = 3.0 m/s.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: total impulse = 6.0 + 18 = 24 N·s = Δp; from rest v = 24/2.0 = 12 m/s.

subtopic: Work–energy theorem with an angled applied force and friction
learningObjective: Apply the work–energy theorem on a horizontal surface, correctly resolving an angled pull into its work-doing horizontal component and its effect on the normal force and friction.
stem: A crate of mass 4.0 kg is initially at rest on a rough horizontal floor. A worker pulls it a distance of 4.0 m along the floor using a rope held at a constant angle above the horizontal, applying a constant force of 25 N along the rope (take cos θ = 0.80 and sin θ = 0.60). The coefficient of kinetic friction between crate and floor is 0.30 and g = 10 m/s². What is the speed of the crate after it has moved 4.0 m?
explanation: Only the horizontal component of the pull does work: W_pull = F cos θ × d = 25 × 0.80 × 4.0 = 80 J. The upward component of the pull lightens the crate, so the normal force is N = mg − F sin θ = 40 − 15 = 25 N; kinetic friction is 0.30 × 25 = 7.5 N, doing W_fric = −7.5 × 4.0 = −30 J. Net work = 80 − 30 = 50 J = ½(4.0)v², so v = 5.0 m/s.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: net work = 80 J − 30 J = 50 J = ½(4.0)v² ⇒ v = 5.0 m/s.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: neglects friction entirely and equates the pull's work (80 J) to the kinetic energy, giving 6.3 m/s.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: uses N = mg and ignores that the upward component of the pull reduces the normal force (and hence friction), giving 4.0 m/s.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses the full force (25 N) rather than its horizontal component F cos θ when computing the work done by the pull, overstating the work as 100 J (v ≈ 5.9 m/s).
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: takes N = mg + F sin θ, treating the rope's upward pull as increasing the normal force; this overestimates friction and gives 2.6 m/s.

subtopic: Energy conservation with friction and a spring on a curved track
learningObjective: Track mechanical energy through a sequence of gravitational, frictional and elastic stages to find the maximum compression of a spring.
stem: A block of mass 2.0 kg is released from rest at a height of 1.8 m on a frictionless curved ramp. At the bottom the ramp joins a horizontal surface. The block first crosses a rough patch of length 3.0 m (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.20) and then reaches an ideal spring (spring constant 1200 N/m) mounted on a smooth section. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is the maximum compression of the spring?
explanation: The gravitational energy released is mgh = 2.0 × 10 × 1.8 = 36 J. Friction on the rough patch dissipates μmgL = 0.20 × 2.0 × 10 × 3.0 = 12 J. The remaining 24 J is stored in the spring at maximum compression: ½kx² = 24 J, so x² = 48/1200 = 0.04 and x = 0.20 m.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: treats μ as a fractional energy loss, storing mgh(1 − μ) = 28.8 J instead of subtracting the friction work μmgL, giving x ≈ 0.22 m.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: mgh − μmgL = 36 − 12 = 24 J = ½(1200)x² ⇒ x = 0.20 m.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: neglects the friction loss on the rough patch and stores the full 36 J in the spring, giving x ≈ 0.24 m.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: adds the friction energy to mgh instead of subtracting it (48 J stored), giving x ≈ 0.28 m.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: omits the factor ½ in the spring energy, setting kx² = 24 J, giving x = √0.02 ≈ 0.14 m.

subtopic: Elastic collision: fraction of kinetic energy transferred
learningObjective: Use the head-on elastic-collision velocity relations to determine the fraction of kinetic energy transferred between unequal masses.
stem: On a frictionless surface, a ball of mass m moving with speed v makes a head-on elastic collision with a stationary ball of mass 3m. After the collision, what fraction of the incident ball's kinetic energy has been transferred to the 3m ball?
explanation: For a head-on elastic collision the struck ball moves off with v₂' = [2m₁/(m₁ + m₂)]v = [2m/(4m)]v = v/2. Its kinetic energy is ½(3m)(v/2)² = 0.375 mv², while the incident energy is ½mv² = 0.5 mv². The fraction transferred is 0.375/0.5 = 0.75, equivalently 4m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)² = 12/16 = 75%.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: squares the velocity ratio (v₂'/v)² = 1/4 but forgets to weight the kinetic energy by the mass 3m, giving 25%.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: v₂' = v/2, so KE₂'/KE_i = 3 × (1/2)² = 3/4 = 75% (= 4m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)²).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: assumes kinetic energy is simply shared equally between the two balls, giving 50%.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: assumes the incident ball stops and gives up all its kinetic energy, which holds only for equal masses, giving 100%.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: assumes the transferred fraction equals the mass ratio m₁/m₂ = 1/3 ≈ 33%.

subtopic: Vertical circular motion over a crest (apparent weight)
learningObjective: Apply Newton's second law in the radial direction at the top of a vertical arc to relate speed to the apparent weight (normal force).
stem: A car travels over the top of a hill whose crest is a circular arc of radius 45 m in a vertical plane. At what speed will the driver experience an apparent weight (the normal force from the seat) equal to half of their true weight? Take g = 10 m/s².
explanation: At the crest, gravity and the normal force both act vertically and provide the centripetal force: mg − N = mv²/R. Setting the apparent weight N = mg/2 gives mg − mg/2 = mv²/R, so v² = gR/2 = 10 × 45 / 2 = 225 and v = 15 m/s.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: sets N = 0 (solves for weightlessness/loss of contact) rather than N = mg/2, giving v = √(gR) ≈ 21 m/s.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: uses v = √(2gR), confusing the circular-motion condition with a free-fall/energy speed, giving 30 m/s.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: mg − N = mv²/R with N = mg/2 ⇒ v = √(gR/2) = √225 = 15 m/s.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses the bottom-of-arc relation N − mg = mv²/R (i.e. mg + N = mv²/R), giving v = √(3gR/2) ≈ 26 m/s.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: halves the loss-of-contact speed √(gR) directly, halving the speed instead of the apparent weight, giving ≈ 10.6 m/s.

subtopic: Orbital energy: work to raise a circular orbit
learningObjective: Use the total-mechanical-energy expression for a circular orbit to determine the energy required to raise an orbit, recognising that kinetic energy decreases while total energy increases.
stem: A small satellite is in a circular orbit around a planet, where its orbital speed is 8.0 km/s. Mission control wishes to transfer it to a new circular orbit of four times the original radius. Treating the manoeuvre as ideal, how much energy per unit mass must be supplied to (or released by) the satellite? (For a circular orbit the total mechanical energy per unit mass is −½v².)
explanation: For a circular orbit v² = GM/r, so quadrupling r halves the orbital speed: v_f = 4.0 km/s. The specific total energy is e = −½v²: e_i = −½(8000)² = −3.2×10⁷ J/kg and e_f = −½(4000)² = −8.0×10⁶ J/kg. The energy that must be supplied per unit mass is Δe = e_f − e_i = +2.4×10⁷ J/kg = 24 MJ/kg. Note that the kinetic energy actually falls, but the potential energy rises by more, so net energy must be added.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: uses the change in kinetic energy (½Δv² = −24 MJ/kg) and interprets the drop in KE as energy released, ignoring the larger rise in potential energy.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: quotes only the magnitude of the initial orbit's total (binding) energy (½v_i² = 32 MJ/kg) instead of the change between orbits.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: uses only the change in gravitational potential energy (ΔU = +48 MJ/kg), ignoring the compensating decrease in kinetic energy.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: e = −½v²; Δe = −8.0×10⁶ − (−3.2×10⁷) = +2.4×10⁷ J/kg, i.e. 24 MJ/kg must be supplied.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: quotes only the magnitude of the final orbit's total energy (½v_f² = 8 MJ/kg), not the change between the two orbits.

subtopic: SHM: amplitude from two speed–displacement data points
learningObjective: Use the SHM relation v² = ω²(A² − x²) with two measured states to solve simultaneously for the angular frequency and amplitude.
stem: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion along a straight line. When its displacement from the equilibrium position is 3.0 cm its speed is 0.40 m/s, and when its displacement is 4.0 cm its speed is 0.30 m/s. What is the amplitude of the motion?
explanation: For SHM the speed obeys v² = ω²(A² − x²). Substituting both states (in SI units): 0.16 = ω²(A² − 0.0009) and 0.09 = ω²(A² − 0.0016). Subtracting eliminates A²: 0.07 = ω²(0.0007), so ω² = 100. Then A² − 0.0009 = 0.16/100 = 0.0016, giving A² = 0.0025 and A = 0.050 m = 5.0 cm.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: assumes the larger displacement, where the speed is smaller, is already the turning point (amplitude), giving 4.0 cm.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: uses the incorrect relation v² ∝ (A − x) rather than v² ∝ (A² − x²), yielding A ≈ 5.3 cm.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: simply adds the two displacements, 3.0 + 4.0 = 7.0 cm.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: takes the amplitude as the average of the two measured displacements, (3.0 + 4.0)/2 = 3.5 cm.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: solving v² = ω²(A² − x²) at both points gives ω² = 100 and A² = 0.0025, so A = 5.0 cm.
